newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cool to U.N. appeal on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cool to U.N. appeal on Iraq.

text.p: The United States reacted cooly on Monday to reports by U.N. aid agencies that thousands of people are at risk this winter because of lack of food, medicine and clean water in Iraq.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the United States has no way of evaluating "the degree of the crisis" in Iraq because it has no diplomats on the ground there.

Besides, the "way to correct the problem of Iraqi malnutrition ... and deprivation on the part of Iraqi citizens (is) for (Iraqi leader) Saddam Hussein to start caring about what happens to his people, instead of building 15 palaces, enriching his family with overseas bank accounts," Burns said.

He was reacting to a news conference in New York at which U.N. aid agencies expressed alarm at the dearth of critical supplies at the onset of winter in Iraq, saying only 4 percent of the funds they asked for had been donated by the international community.

Burns said the adminstration has long felt "the Iraqi people have suffered because of Saddam Hussein's rule" and that is why Washington co-authored U.N. resolution 986 which aimed to bring food and medicine to Iraqi people under an oil-for-food plan.

But the U.N. resolution was held up after Saddam sent troops into northern Iraq to intervene in fighting between Kurdish factions and even now Saddam is "not working cooperatively with the United Nations" in trying to revive the oil-for-food programme, he said.

"If he (Saddam) ... started taking some of that personal fortune and maybe spending it on his own population, then I think the Iraqi people would be better off. And if he didn't throw roadblocks in the way of the United Nations, U.N. Resolution 986 could have gone forward long ago," Burns said.

Burns insisted Washington is not insensitive to the Iraqi people's suffering and officials would discuss with the U.N. aid agencies the data on which they drew their conclusions about a looming crisis in Iraq. But he mostly blamed Saddam for the situation.

In New York, Catherine Bertini, director of the U.N. World Food Programme, said: "The humanitarian situation throughout Iraq is dismal, and with the onset of winter will become critical for tens of thousands of women children and other Iraqis who already are living well below the poverty level."

Of the $39.9 million requested in a September appeal only $1.6 million was received, from the Netherlands and from France, Yasushi Akashi, the undersecretary-general for humanitarian affairs, told the news conference.

Akashi said one reason for the paucity of funds was the expectation that the oil-for-food plan would go into effect soon. This arrangement, still to be implemented, allows Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil to purchase food, medicine and other necessities in scarce supply since U.N. sanctions were imposed in August 1990. Humanitarian goods are exempt.

Bertini said she needed $19 million for 2.15 million "highly vulnerable" people, including 900,000 war widows, 180,000 malnourished children under five and 200,000 pregnant or nursing mothers. UNICEF needs $10 million for essential medicine and food supplement for children suffering from disease and malnutrition.
